issues.detail: The two examples mostly point back to earlier code blocks and show a single run command each, so they are thin demonstrations: the AI agent example is never run, and the batch loop example uses undeclared variables (nightly, getPending, finish, enrichContact, saveContact).

scenarios.name: branching-lead-router-with-validation
scenarios.rationale: Response A uses the SDK's generic trigger/node/ifElse factories, wires the branches with .onTrue/.onFalse under workflow().add().to(), builds the conditions object with options, conditions and combinator, uses expr() for the left value, and calls .validate() and .toJSON(). Response B hand-writes raw n8n JSON with no SDK factories, no .onTrue/.onFalse and no .validate(), and its own validation is a custom script.

scenarios.name: ai-agent-memory-session-key
scenarios.rationale: A matches every rubric point, including nodeJson(support, 'body.userId') for the memory session key; B uses expr('{{ $json.body.userId }}') for the session key, which the rubric specifically rules out, though B does get the other items right, such as the $fromAI query parameter, the system message, and newCredential.

scenarios.name: json-to-code-and-deploy
scenarios.rationale: Response A uses generateWorkflowCode, parseWorkflowCode and validateWorkflow with a result.valid check that prints errors and exits 1. It also POSTs only name, nodes, connections and settings with the X-N8N-API-KEY header and publishes via /publish. It pins the version with --save-exact and reads the key from an env var. Response B uses the deprecated /activate endpoint, has no --save-exact pin, and hedges on the SDK function names, though it does read the key from an env var and the other scripts are mostly sound.
